name: BitLib
workload: Google Benchmark micro-benchmarks of STL-style algorithms (set, shift_left/right, reverse, transform (unary/binary), rotate, count, swap_ranges, copy, equal, move, copy_backward, fill, find) over bit containers of size 2^8 (small) through 2^31 (huge) bits, run against bit::bit_vector, pinam45/dynamic_bitset, noporpoise/BitArray, and std::vector<bool>.
claimed_speedup: bit::shift_left ~283x faster than std::shift_left at large size (371,224 ns vs 105,227,752 ns, derived from page data); bit::reverse ~236x faster at large size (1,245,260 ns vs 293,563,397 ns, derived); bit::count ~161x faster at large size (365,194 ns vs 58,934,071 ns, derived); bit::rotate ~70x faster at large size (7,333,284 ns vs 514,697,313 ns, derived); bit::set ~1.26x faster at large size (1.90 ns vs 2.39 ns, derived)
tradeoffs: Header-only, C++17+; bit_vector wraps std::vector<WordType> and mirrors std::vector<bool>'s interface, but the speedups only apply when using BitLib's own bit::-namespaced algorithms (bit::rotate, bit::transform, etc.) instead of <algorithm>; optional SIMD path requires opting into Google Highway (BITLIB_HWY).
caveats: This is the assignment's known lead. The README's benchmark table has no stated compiler flags or CPU model, so tier is capped at C even though the benchmark code (Google Benchmark, BITLIB_BENCHMARK CMake option) is public. Several ratios exceed 50x (shift_left, reverse, transform at 'large' sizes), which is plausible given std::vector<bool>'s well-documented bit-by-bit iteration cost in libstdc++/libc++, but cannot be independently verified without stated methodology. 11 open issues; last commit 2024-06-06 (stale).
found_via: GitHub: assignment's known lead (bkille/BitLib); confirmed via `gh api repos/bkille/BitLib` and its README "Performance Benchmarks" section

name: sul::dynamic_bitset
workload: Same third-party Google Benchmark suite as BitLib (shift_left/right, transform, count, fill) at 'small' (256-bit) and 'large' (16,777,216-bit) sizes, comparing sul::dynamic_bitset against std::vector<bool>.
claimed_speedup: shift_left (small): 13.1 ns vs std 345 ns, ~26x (derived from page data); shift_left (large): 638,896 ns vs std 105,227,752 ns, ~165x (derived); count (small): 6.29 ns vs std 234 ns, ~37x (derived); count (large): 365,279 ns vs std 58,934,071 ns, ~161x (derived); fill (small): 4.79 ns vs std 9.15 ns, ~1.9x (derived)
tradeoffs: Header-only C++17/20 alternative to boost::dynamic_bitset; dynamic size like std::vector<bool> (not fixed-size like std::bitset); optionally links kimwalisch/libpopcnt for faster counting; narrower feature set than boost::dynamic_bitset.
caveats: Numbers are harvested from a third party's (bkille/BitLib) own README benchmark table, not from dynamic_bitset's own repo or its companion pinam45/dynamic_bitset_benchmarks repo (which contains no published numeric results, only a set-covering-problem test harness). No compiler flags or CPU model stated anywhere in the source; several ratios exceed 50x, so tier is capped at C per the implausible-ratio rule.
found_via: GitHub: harvested as a named winner from bkille/BitLib's README benchmark shootout table (dynamic_bitset:: rows); cross-checked via `gh api repos/pinam45/dynamic_bitset`

name: pasta::bit_vector
baseline: cs-poppy (Zhou, Andersen & Kaminsky, SEA'13 compact rank/select bit-vector structure)
workload: rank and select queries on a length-n uncompressed bit vector, at ~3.51% space overhead
claimed_speedup: up to 8% faster rank and up to 16.5% faster select vs cs-poppy, at equal space overhead
tradeoffs: Header-only C++20; GPL-3.0 is more restrictive than MIT/BSD peers; adds rank/select operations that std::bitset/std::vector<bool> lack entirely, so it's an additive capability rather than a drop-in replacement; fastest variant relies on SIMD and -march=native.
caveats: std::bitset/std::vector<bool> have no native rank/select, so there is no direct std baseline for this functionality; the recorded baseline (cs-poppy) is the field's standard compact rank/select structure (Zhou et al., SEA'13), not a mainstream stdlib facility, which is why baseline_in_list=false and confidence is capped. This is a peer-reviewed paper (Kurpicz, SPIRE 2022) with public benchmark code (github.com/pasta-toolbox/bit_vector_experiments), but the exact compiler flags and CPU model used for the paper's reported numbers were not confirmed on the pages opened this session (only generic CMake build presets were found in the repo README), so it is scored B rather than A.
found_via: GitHub: `gh search repos "succinct data structure" --language c++ --sort stars` -> pasta-toolbox/bit_vector; claim verified against paper abstract at arxiv.org/abs/2206.01149
